content.title: Interesting investigation of discrete latent variable in VAE objective, but limited discussion.
content.review:
This paper describes an optimal transport approach for learning autoencoders with discrete and continuous latent variables.
Wasserstein autoencoder (WAE) is developed for better use of the discrete latent variable.
Experiments using MNIST dataset show how it works.

Strong point of the paper: 
The empirical investigation to the reason why discrete latent variable is discarded in the VAE objective is interesting.

Weak points:
* The evaluation is limited to only MNIST datasets.
* What encourages the use of latent variable is unclear (see below).

The reviewer has several questions and comments.
* The choice of \lambda may depend on the dimensionality of x. I am curious how this affects when applied to other datasets.
* WAE is different from VAE in three ways: 
(1) l2 reconstruction error written as \|x - y\|_2^2, 
(2) MMD with IMQ kernels instead of KL divergence between variational distribution q and prior p, and 
(3) latent variable k being marginalized out.
The paper should elaborate more on which factor heps the use of discrete latent variable.
* Figure 5 (c) is hard to read. Different marker shape (rather than its size) should improve the clarity to distinguish the samples from P and Q.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Clarification of latent-usage driver
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their feedback.

We indeed tuned the parameters on the MNIST data and acknowledge that lambda is chosen empirically. For example, in Tolstikhin et al. (2018), the authors set lambda to 10 on the CelebA data set. Adler & Lunz (2018) propose some heuristics for the choice of the regularization parameter. It is worth remembering that in theory, lambda should tend to infinity in order to recover the true Wasserstein distance.

(1) The WAE framework can be used with any cost functions, and while the Euclidean distance seems the most natural when working with image-type data, there exist many norm or cost functions more adapted to vision application (See Adler & Lunz (2018) for some cost examples). For example, Patrini et al. (2018) chose the cross entropy loss for the MNIST data set. On the contrary, the VAE framework enforces to use the expected log reconstruction under the variational distribution as the reconstruction cost. One consequence is that the WAE reconstruction term is model independent and especially, allows for deterministic models, which has been long seen as a limitation of the VAE framework (Hoffman & Johnson, 2016 ). However, the authors want to emphasis that the collapse to the prior mode in the VAE seems to be mainly due to the regularization term in the VAE objective Eq. (2) and less to the choice of cost function in the reconstruction term.

(2) Here again, the choice for the regularization term is flexible. The WAE framework just requires a valid divergence function between distributions whereas the VAE imposes the use of the KL divergence. However, the real difference between the two frameworks is the distributions which are being regularized. While the VAE objective regularizes the variational distribution at a data-point level to the prior, the WAE objective regularizes the aggregated variational distribution to the prior (see Eq. (6)). It is the per-data-point regularization that seems to be at the origin of the variational distribution modes collapse in the VAE framework whereas the WAE only pushes the variational distribution to match the prior in an aggregated manner.

(3) The authors are not sure of the meaning of this question. In the two approaches, the same models have been considered, and in both cases, the marginalization over the discrete latent is necessary to apply the reparameterization trick. 

Finally, we have updated the marker shape in Figure 5c to improve readability.

content.title: ok work, would like to see fairer evaluation.
content.review:
The authors show that using VAE framework using a generative model with a mixture-of-Gaussians latent variable structure does not work naively. They propose a wasserstein-based objective that is better amenable to optimization and showed good qualitative/quantitative results on mnist dataset. I like the presentation of the work, especially answering some of my obvious questions like what happens if the VAE is initialized with wasserstein objective. 

I'm on the fence about acceptance due to the following 2 questions

(a) do we really need to impose a structured distribution, i.e. gaussian latent variable structure with K centers. Would'nt using K times as many parameters with a single gaussian distribution and a neural network 'g' (using notation in Kingma & Welling) not be expressive enough to capture the data distribution ? 

(b) one of the authors main explanation on why the collapse of the K to 1 occurs is that "discrete KL term is negligible". Given that the MMD term in eq(4) is weighted by \lambda, could the authors have not chosen to weight the KL term by lambda as well ? 

I would like the authors to present the results of (a) and (b) to give the baseline VAE an equal footing with the author's proposal.

content.title: Discussion of why our comparison is the right comparison
content.comment:
We appreciate the feedback provided by the reviewer.

In this work, the authors try to show that the WAE (Tolstikhin et al., 2018) framework is more adapted to generative modelling as it allows better convergence of densities. Thus, the fact that the MoG-latent VAE does not converge well where the MoG-latent WAE does is more important than showing that the MoG-latent WAE performance is better than all other models with the same number of parameters. Furthermore, the structure of the data is given by 10 digit classes and this prior knowledge suggests that the density of the data should be concentrated on 10 different modes. Therefore, a prior with a MoG structure is more naturally motivated by the problem at hand than a single Gaussian. 

Indeed, by using such a structured prior, the task of encoding the data is split, with the discrete encoder having to learn the global structure of the data (the different modes) while the continuous encoders only need to capture the structure within each mode. It should be noted that this model choice, combined with the WAE framework, enable the use of relatively simple networks (3 layers DCGAN-style network for the discrete encoder, 32-unit two-hidden-layer mlp networks for the K continuous encoders and 3-layer DCGAN-style network for the decoder network) keeping the number of parameters relatively low. 

Secondly, the VAE objective Eq. (2) and WAE objective Eq. (6) indeed present similarities. Both are composed of a reconstruction cost and a regularization term. In the case of WAE, the actual regularization comes from a Lagrangien-type relaxation of a strong constraint on the infimum set for the variational distribution. Thus, the weight in the WAE is free and can be tuned at training time, with theoretical guarantee in the infinite limit. On the contrary, in the VAE objective, the weight is fixed to 1 by construction of the objective. So these two terms are fundamentally different. However, some works have proposed to re-weight the KL penalization cost in the VAE objective (Higgins et al., 2016) to rebalanced the two terms in Eq. (2). With this re-weighting of the penalization, the theoretical guarantees of the ELBO are lost, but it does allow for more flexibility in the relative weighting of the reconstruction term and the penalization term. Comparisons with both the original VAE objective Eq. (2) and re-weighted objectives are given Fig. 4d for different weight values, beta. While the re-weighting of the regularization term impacts the VAE performance, the authors found that it does not prevent the mode-collapse issue.

content.title: Paper needs to be tightened with regard to the exact problem we're trying to solve and how we measure success
content.review:
- There are several things about the presentation I find confusing.  There are two different objective functions you're considering: the ones based on the 2-Wasserstein distance in equations (3), (4), and (6), and the VAE in equation (2).  So what are you referring to in the abstract when you say "we find our discrete latent variable to be fully leveraged by the model when trained, without any modifications to the objective function or significant fine tuning".  It seems like you're using a different objective function, so what do you mean by "without any modification"?

- On page 1 you state that "we seek also to establish that training generative models with OT can be significantly more effective than the traditional VAE approach."  Yet you don't really say how you measure this effectiveness.  Very late in the paper, on p7, you suggest using the reconstruction loss from the VAE objective to compare the trained models.  Is this the answer?  If so, I think you need to move it way up in the paper and give some discussion on why this makes sense as an evaluation metric.

- At least a couple times you refer to wanting to get a "weaker topology", which I know is an idea developed in Bousquet et al's 2017 paper.  But you should include at least some explanation of what you mean by this and its implications -- "weak topology" seems like a pretty fancy term for the mathematical level of this paper.  In first paragraph of section 2.2, what is the "induced topology" of maximum likelihood?

- To further elucidate the crux of the issue in Section 2.1, it might be helpful to explain why the EM algorithm, which is just an ELBO maximizer, for basic Gaussian mixture models doesn't typically have issues with a collapsing mixing distribution.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Clarifications provided
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their feedback. We attempt to address the main criticism, which was the lack of precision in the specification of the problem that we are solving in this work.

In this paper we show that the WAE framework is able to better train a generative model with MOG prior than the VAE framework. The WAE objective that we use is the standard one given in Eq. (6), which is derived by plugging our model from Eq. (1), and the variational distribution into the WAE objective given in Eq. (4) of Tolstikhin et al. (2018). The steps from Eqs. (3) and (4) were meant as a review of how Eq. (6) is derived, not as alternatives. We are able to train our MOG latent-variable model with this standard WAE objective, hence our statement in the abstract.

For comparison, the authors trained the same model as a VAE (Kingma & Welling, 2014) as a baseline. While, we mainly discuss and compare these two methods, we also used a modified version of the VAE objective Eq. (2) where the KL regularization term is weighted to mirror the regularization weight in WAE objective, as it has been proposed in several works (Higgins et al., 2016). However, the re-weighting of the penalization term in the VAE objective is a fundamental modification as it destroys the lower bound of the log likelihood (ELBO) of the model. Moreover, as in Higgins et al. (2016), this reweighting gives the best results when using an increasing scheme during training. On the contrary, the regularization weighting Eq. (6) does not need special tuning beside a rough grid search over the value of this regularization weight.

Our primary demonstration of the effectiveness of our OT approach versus the traditional VAE is that all but one of the discrete latent modes in the VAE collapse, which is not the case for the WAE. This is discussed extensively on page 2. We attempted to go further by looking at the VAE reconstruction loss Eq. (2) and the accuracy as a measure of the latent fidelity as in Makhzani et al. (2016). The experiment presented Fig. 4c shows that the WAE is indeed better at reconstructing in a VAE sense, even when it has not been trained to do so. The experiment shown Fig. 5b pictures how the WAE method makes the training of the generative model better at leveraging the structure of the prior. 

In this paper, the authors deliberated chose to keep hidden the mathematical burden of the Optimal Transport approach for clarity. In Arjovsky et al. (2017), the authors go deeper into the mathematical details of the OT approach to generative modelling. The main take away from the discussion is that the Wasserstein distance should enable easier convergence of distributions than the KL divergence. The high-level idea being that the Wasserstein distance yields a weaker topology than the pseudo topology induced by the KL divergence, and the stronger the topology, the harder it is for a sequence to converge. In other words, the convergence of a sequence in a stronger topology implies the convergence of this sequence in a weaker topology. The other way around does not hold. We have added a comment to this effect into the paper to make it clear why a weaker topology is helpful.

The authors acknowledge the abusive use of the notion of topology when referencing the topology induced by maximum likelihood (i.e. the KL). Indeed, the KL divergence is not a proper distance function (not symmetric), and thus cannot induced a topology in its mathematical definition. However, Theoreme 2.3 of Arjovsky et al. (2017) shows that the set of convergent sequences of distributions in a KL sense contains the set of convergent sequences in a total-variation sense. That is, the convergence in a KL sense implies the convergence in a total-variation sense.  Thus, we abusively say that the “topology induced” by the KL is stronger than the topology induced by the total-variation distance, itself stronger than the weak topology induced by Wasserstein distance. 

The EM algorithm is indeed a very efficient ELBO maximizer when the posterior is tractable and mean-field type variational distribution is used. In the E-step of the EM algorithm, the variational distribution is set equal to the posterior of the model, thus prohibiting the variational distribution from collapsing to one mode of the prior. However, in many cases, and especially, when the generative part of the model is parametrized by a nonlinear function, the posterior becomes intractable, and thus the E-steps breaks down. Some modification of this EM algorithm, where a partial E-step is performed by taking gradient steps have been proposed to deal with intractable posteriors. While the authors didn’t not implement this algorithm, they believe that the partial E-step will lead to the same local minima for the variational distribution where all the probability mass of the variational distribution is pushed onto a single mode of the prior.
